rationale: The standard requires students to share relevant and accurate information through a variety of different modes (C). Students share relevant, accurate information about the sun, moon, stars, and Earth's rotation orally during the Back-to-Back and Face-to-Face protocol ("I would like to add _____") and during whole-group responses describing photographs ("yellow, hidden"; "sliver, white"). The relevance and accuracy clauses are met by these student-performed oral contributions grounded in the text, poem, and video. However, the "variety of different modes" clause is only partially met: the dominant student mode is oral sharing (partner talk, whole-group responses), while the written component is teacher-scribed shared writing where the teacher completes the recording form using student ideas — the students do not independently produce written text as a second mode. A future lesson where students write in their own Sky notebooks would likely strengthen this clause.

rationale: ⚑ REVIEW: none-or-partial — The comprehension (I) clauses are met: students practice multiple comprehension strategies across the lesson, including distinguishing information from illustrations vs. text ("What is something you learned from an illustration … I saw a picture of the earth spinning"), activating background knowledge (recalling sitting in a shadow), identifying adjectives in a poem ("What were some adjectives that you heard to describe the sun, moon, or stars?" — "sun: hot, moon: full, stars: twinkling"), and discussing observations from a video via the Back-to-Back and Face-to-Face protocol. The lesson builds toward independent Sky notebook writing in the next lesson but does not reach it here.

The explain clause is partially met: students demonstrate understanding of how adjectives are used by generating adjectives to describe photographs ("yellow, hidden," "sliver, white") and by connecting adjectives to real-world objects ("What is something at home or at school that we could describe using this adjective?" — "a bowl of soup; the nightlight"), but no activity explicitly asks students to explain the purpose, effect, or function of descriptive words within the text.
